html:
The multichannel cochlear implant is an electronic device that lets many deaf people hear. In 1978 a team led by the surgeon Graeme Clark at the University of Melbourne fitted the first one.

The device works by skipping the damaged hair cells of the inner ear. A microphone picks up sound, a processor splits it into frequency bands, and a row of electrodes in the cochlea stimulates the hearing nerve at different points, one band to each place. Earlier single-channel implants, such as those of William House in the United States, could give a sense of rhythm but little speech. Clark's many channels let people understand words.

The first patient, Rod Saunders, had lost his hearing in an accident. The design was taken up by the Australian company Cochlear, founded in 1981, and became one of Australia's best-known inventions. Hundreds of thousands of people now use cochlear implants, many of them children born deaf.
